title: Nebraska Civics & Government (12th Grade)
description: Nebraska Civics & Government (12th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: A Nebraska student reads that the opening words of the U.S. Constitution are 'We the People.' Those words announce that government power comes from:
questions.explanation: The Preamble grounds the Constitution in popular sovereignty: authority flows from the people, who grant powers through the Constitution and can change it by amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: People first: power starts with We the People.

img.scene: An open book representing a constitution on a wooden table in soft daylight, quill beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: People first: power starts with We the People.
img.title: WE THE PEOPLE

questions.question: Under the U.S. Constitution, the branch that makes federal laws is:
questions.correctAnswer: Congress - the Senate and the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: Article I vests legislative power in Congress, a bicameral body of Senate and House. The President enforces laws and the courts interpret them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Makers sit in Congress.

img.scene: A grand legislative chamber with two curved rows of empty desks and chairs, flags at the front. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Makers sit in Congress.
img.title: CONGRESS MAKES LAWS

questions.question: A Nebraska civics class watches the news: both houses of Congress passed a bill, the President vetoed it, and the anchors say Congress may yet make it law. That can happen only if:
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of each house votes to override the veto
distractors: A majority of the Supreme Court agrees
The Vice President signs it instead
It passes one house again by simple majority
questions.explanation: The veto-override rule in Article I requires two-thirds of both the House and the Senate, a deliberately high bar that keeps overrides rare.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds can override.

img.scene: A large document on a desk with a red veto stamp shape beside it and rows of raised hands in a chamber behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds can override.
img.title: THE VETO OVERRIDE

questions.question: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution are known together as:
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1791, the first ten amendments protect individual rights such as speech, religion, and due process against the federal government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: First ten: Bill of Rights.

img.scene: Ten aged parchment scrolls arranged in a row on a dark table, candles nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: First ten: Bill of Rights.
img.title: BILL OF RIGHTS

questions.question: A student lists five freedoms - speaking her mind, worshiping freely, publishing a school paper, joining a peaceful rally, and asking the government to fix a problem. A single amendment shields all five. Which one?
questions.explanation: The First Amendment bars Congress from establishing a religion or abridging free exercise, speech, press, assembly, and petition.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms, First Amendment.

img.scene: A town square scene with a small church, a newspaper stand, and people peacefully gathering. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms, First Amendment.
img.title: FIRST AMENDMENT FREEDOMS

questions.question: Before officers may enter and search a family's house looking for evidence, the Fourth Amendment ordinarily obliges them to get which of the following from a judge first?
questions.correctAnswer: A warrant based on probable cause, describing the place and items sought
distractors: A two-thirds vote of the city council
A warrant only if the owner is home
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment bans unreasonable searches and requires warrants issued on probable cause that particularly describe what may be searched or seized.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Search needs a warrant.

img.scene: A front door of a house with a judge signing a paper at a desk in the background scene. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Search needs a warrant.
img.title: FOURTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A defendant refuses to testify at her own criminal trial. The protection she is using comes from:
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination
distractors: The Sixth Amendment speedy trial right
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment provides that no person shall be compelled in a criminal case to be a witness against himself; it also guarantees due process and grand jury indictment for serious federal crimes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Silent under the Fifth.

img.scene: A courtroom with an empty witness chair and a judge looking toward it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Silent under the Fifth.
img.title: FIFTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a criminal defendant all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.correctAnswer: A guaranteed acquittal if the trial is delayed
distractors: The assistance of counsel for the defense
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees speedy public trial, impartial jury, notice of charges, confrontation of witnesses, and counsel - but never guarantees an outcome.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sixth: fair trial tools, no promised verdict.

img.scene: A courtroom interior with jury box, witness stand and counsel tables, empty. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Sixth: fair trial tools, no promised verdict.
img.title: SIXTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A formerly enslaved man's freedom became permanent nationwide - not just a wartime measure - when which amendment was ratified in 1865?
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1865 after the Civil War, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for a crime.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thirteen ended slavery.

img.scene: Broken iron chains lying on a wooden surface in warm light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Thirteen ended slavery.
img.title: THIRTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: Citizenship for all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and equal protection of the laws, are defined in:
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) defines national and state citizenship and bars states from denying due process or equal protection.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fourteen: citizenship and equal protection.

img.scene: A newborn baby footprint beside a courthouse column in soft light, symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Fourteen: citizenship and equal protection.
img.title: FOURTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: The Fifteenth Amendment prohibits denying the right to vote based on:
questions.correctAnswer: Race, color, or previous condition of servitude
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment targets racial discrimination in voting; age rules come from state law and the Twenty-sixth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteen: vote cannot turn on race.

img.scene: A ballot box with hands of different skin tones placing ballots into it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Fifteen: vote cannot turn on race.
img.title: FIFTEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: Women's suffrage was established nationwide by:
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1920, the Nineteenth Amendment bars denying the vote on account of sex.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nineteen: women vote nationwide.

img.scene: Women in early 1900s dress placing ballots into a wooden ballot box. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Nineteen: women vote nationwide.
img.title: NINETEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A 19-year-old soldier in 1971 could be drafted but, in many states, still could not vote. The constitutional change that fixed that nationwide set the voting age at:
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1971 during the Vietnam era, the Twenty-sixth Amendment set 18 as the voting age floor states may not exceed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Vote at eighteen.

img.scene: A young voter receiving a ballot at a polling place table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Vote at eighteen.
img.title: VOTING AGE

questions.question: Under the Constitution, a person must be at least how old to serve in the U.S. Senate?
questions.explanation: Article I sets Senate qualifications: at least 30 years old, nine years a U.S. citizen, and an inhabitant of the state represented.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senate starts at thirty.

img.scene: A dignified chamber with long desks in curved rows, empty seats. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Senate starts at thirty.
img.title: SENATE AGE

questions.question: Members of the U.S. House of Representatives are elected for terms of:
questions.explanation: House members face voters every two years, making the House the chamber most frequently accountable to the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House: every two years.

img.scene: Voters queuing at a polling station in a school gymnasium. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House: every two years.
img.title: HOUSE TERMS

questions.question: Each state's number of seats in the U.S. House is based mainly on:
questions.correctAnswer: The state's population, counted in the census every ten years
questions.explanation: Article I apportions House seats by population after each decennial census; every state gets at least one seat.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House seats follow people.

img.scene: Census workers with clipboards walking a neighborhood street. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House seats follow people.
img.title: APPORTIONMENT

questions.question: A state's total number of electoral votes for President equals:
questions.correctAnswer: Its number of U.S. senators plus its number of U.S. representatives
distractors: Its number of U.S. representatives only
questions.explanation: Each state gets electors equal to its full congressional delegation - House seats (population-based) plus two senators.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Electors equal the delegation.

img.scene: A map-like arrangement of state-shaped wooden blocks on a table, no labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Electors equal the delegation.
img.title: ELECTORAL VOTES

questions.question: To win the presidency through the Electoral College, a candidate needs at least:
distractors: A majority of the popular vote in every state
All the electoral votes of the largest state
questions.explanation: With 538 electors total, 270 is the majority required; if no one reaches it, the House decides among the top candidates.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 270 wins the White House.

img.scene: A finish line ribbon across a road with a white house in the far distance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: 270 wins the White House.
img.title: 270 TO WIN

questions.question: Election night ends with no candidate holding an electoral majority. The Twelfth Amendment sends the decision to which body, voting by state delegation?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives, voting by state delegation
questions.explanation: Under the Twelfth Amendment, the House chooses the President from the top three electoral vote-getters, each state delegation casting one vote.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No majority? The House decides.

img.scene: A chamber of representatives seated in grouped state sections. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No majority? The House decides.
img.title: HOUSE DECIDES

questions.question: A job-description poster for the presidency lists four items. One of them does NOT belong to the President at all. Which item is it?
distractors: Commander in chief of the armed forces
questions.explanation: Only Congress may declare war (Article I). The President commands the military, pardons federal offenses, and makes treaties with two-thirds Senate consent.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: War is declared by Congress.

img.scene: A presidential desk with a telephone, flags and a military map in background, blurred. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: War is declared by Congress.
img.title: PRESIDENTIAL POWERS

questions.question: Franklin Roosevelt's four elections led the nation to cap presidential service in the Twenty-second Amendment. Under that cap, a person may be elected President at most:
questions.explanation: The Twenty-second Amendment (1951) limits a person to two elections as President, with a partial-term rule capping total service just under ten years.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two terms, then done.

img.scene: An hourglass on a desk beside a flag. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two terms, then done.
img.title: TERM LIMITS

questions.question: If the President dies in office, the next in the line of succession is:
distractors: The President pro tempore of the Senate
questions.explanation: The Vice President succeeds first, under Article II as clarified by the Twenty-fifth Amendment; the Speaker follows in the statutory line after the Vice President.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: VP is next in line.

img.scene: A row of empty official chairs in descending order in a formal room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: VP is next in line.
img.title: SUCCESSION

questions.question: Federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, are nominated by the President and confirmed by:
questions.explanation: The Appointments Clause gives nomination to the President and advice and consent to the Senate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senate confirms judges.

img.scene: A hearing room with a long table, microphones and an empty witness chair. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Senate confirms judges.
img.title: JUDICIAL CONFIRMATION

questions.question: The power of judicial review - declaring laws unconstitutional - was firmly established for the Supreme Court in:
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Marshall's opinion in Marbury v. Madison claimed the courts' power to refuse to enforce a law that conflicts with the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury made review real.

img.scene: An old courtroom scene from the early 1800s, judges in robes at a bench. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Marbury made review real.
img.title: MARBURY V MADISON

questions.question: Supreme Court justices serve:
questions.correctAnswer: During good behavior - effectively for life, unless they resign, retire, or are impeached and removed
questions.explanation: Article III's good-behavior tenure insulates federal judges from political pressure; no justice has ever been removed by impeachment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Judges serve for life tenure.

img.scene: Nine empty high-backed chairs behind a long curved bench in a courtroom. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Judges serve for life tenure.
img.title: LIFE TENURE

questions.question: Four justices want to grant review of a lower-court case while five of their colleagues do not. Under the Court's own working practice, known by which name, the case is still heard?
questions.explanation: By Court practice, four of the nine justices voting to grant certiorari puts a case on the docket, even though five are needed to decide it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four votes grant a hearing.

img.scene: Four raised hands among a row of seated robed figures seen from behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Four votes grant a hearing.
img.title: RULE OF FOUR

questions.question: Powers not delegated to the federal government nor prohibited to the states are reserved to the states or the people by:
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment states the federalism default: undelegated, unprohibited powers stay with states or the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tenth: the rest is reserved.

img.scene: A balance scale with a capitol dome on one side and a statehouse on the other, level. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Tenth: the rest is reserved.
img.title: TENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: When a valid federal law conflicts with a state law, the federal law prevails under:
distractors: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties the supreme law of the land, binding state judges despite contrary state law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal law is supreme.

img.scene: Two overlapping documents on a desk, the larger one on top, in dramatic light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Federal law is supreme.
img.title: SUPREMACY CLAUSE

questions.question: Congress's power to make all laws 'necessary and proper' for carrying out its listed powers comes from:
questions.correctAnswer: The elastic clause at the end of Article I, Section 8
questions.explanation: The Necessary and Proper Clause stretches Congress's reach to means that carry its enumerated powers into execution - the basis for implied powers upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elastic clause stretches power.

img.scene: A stretched rubber band between two wooden pegs labeled by shape only. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Elastic clause stretches power.
img.title: ELASTIC CLAUSE

questions.question: The system that keeps any one branch from dominating the others, by giving each branch tools to check the others, is called:
questions.explanation: Veto, override, confirmation, impeachment, and judicial review are the working tools of checks and balances layered over separation of powers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Each branch checks the rest.

img.scene: Three interlocking stone pillars supporting a single roof beam. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Each branch checks the rest.
img.title: CHECKS AND BALANCES

questions.question: Impeachment of a federal official begins in the House; the trial and removal vote take place in:
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate, with two-thirds required to convict
distractors: The full Congress in joint session
questions.explanation: The House impeaches by majority; the Senate tries, and conviction and removal require two-thirds of senators present. The Chief Justice presides when the President is tried.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House charges, Senate tries.

img.scene: A formal chamber with a presiding officer and rows of seated members, solemn mood. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House charges, Senate tries.
img.title: IMPEACHMENT

questions.question: A civics textbook diagram shows two different starting gates for a constitutional amendment, both inside Article V. Amendments may be proposed by which pair of routes?
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention called by Congress at the request of two-thirds of state legislatures
distractors: A majority of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Article V provides the two proposal routes; every amendment so far has come through Congress. Ratification needs three-fourths of the states.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article Five: how amendments start.

img.scene: State flags arranged in a semicircle around a central document table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Article Five: how amendments start.
img.title: AMENDING THE CONSTITUTION

questions.question: An amendment becomes part of the U.S. Constitution when ratified by:
questions.explanation: Article V requires ratification by legislatures or conventions in three-fourths of the states - 38 of the current 50.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three-fourths ratify.

img.scene: Hands placing a sealed envelope into a large wooden box in a statehouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Three-fourths ratify.
img.title: RATIFICATION

questions.question: Independence Day fireworks celebrate the date the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration. That adoption date was:
questions.explanation: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration on July 4, 1776; the Constitution was signed in 1787 and ratified in 1788.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: July fourth, seventeen seventy-six.

img.scene: Fireworks over a colonial-era harbor town at dusk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: July fourth, seventeen seventy-six.
img.title: INDEPENDENCE DAY

questions.question: The Constitution was written at the convention held in 1787 in:
questions.explanation: Delegates met in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787, originally to revise the Articles and instead drafted a new Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Philadelphia, seventeen eighty-seven.

img.scene: Delegates in 1700s dress around a long table in a brick hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Philadelphia, seventeen eighty-seven.
img.title: PHILADELPHIA CONVENTION

questions.question: The plan that based representation in Congress on population, favoring large states, was the:
questions.explanation: The Virginia Plan proposed population-based representation in both houses; the small-state New Jersey Plan wanted equality. The Connecticut Compromise split the difference.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Virginia Plan: by population.

img.scene: A large state-shaped wooden block beside smaller blocks on a convention table, no labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Virginia Plan: by population.
img.title: VIRGINIA PLAN

questions.question: The Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise) settled the representation fight by creating:
questions.correctAnswer: A House based on population and a Senate with equal state representation
distractors: One house based only on population
One house with equal representation only
questions.explanation: The compromise produced today's bicameral Congress: proportional House, equal Senate - the same structural question Nebraska later answered differently for its own legislature.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two houses, two logics.

img.scene: Two different sized meeting rooms side by side in a capitol building cutaway. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two houses, two logics.
img.title: GREAT COMPROMISE

questions.question: The Federalist Papers were written mainly to persuade the public to support:
questions.explanation: Hamilton, Madison, and Jay published the essays in 1787-88, chiefly aimed at New York's ratification debate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federalist Papers sold ratification.

img.scene: A stack of newspapers on an 18th century printing press table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Federalist Papers sold ratification.
img.title: FEDERALIST PAPERS

questions.question: At a ratifying convention, an opponent of the new Constitution rises and complains that the document, as written, fails to protect the people's liberties in one specific way. His central objection was that it:
questions.correctAnswer: Lacked a bill of rights protecting individual liberties
distractors: Mentioned the people in its Preamble
questions.explanation: The missing bill of rights was the Anti-Federalists' central charge; the promise to add one helped secure ratification, and the Bill of Rights followed in 1791.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No rights list - that was the fight.

img.scene: A speaker gesturing to a crowd outside a statehouse in colonial dress. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No rights list - that was the fight.
img.title: ANTI-FEDERALIST OBJECTION

questions.question: A Topeka family challenged school segregation, and in 1954 the Supreme Court answered unanimously. The Court's holding in that case, Brown v. Board of Education, was that:
questions.correctAnswer: Racial segregation in public schools is unconstitutional
distractors: States may set separate railway cars
The federal government may not fund schools
questions.explanation: Brown unanimously rejected 'separate but equal' in public education, overturning Plessy's application to schools and driving desegregation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Brown ended school segregation law.

img.scene: Children of different backgrounds walking together up school steps. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Brown ended school segregation law.
img.title: BROWN V BOARD

questions.question: An arrested suspect is about to be questioned in custody. Because of the Supreme Court's 1966 Miranda decision, officers must first:
questions.correctAnswer: Warn arrested suspects of their rights to silence and to an attorney before custodial questioning
distractors: Obtain a search warrant for every arrest
questions.explanation: The Miranda warnings protect the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and the Sixth Amendment right to counsel during custodial interrogation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Miranda: rights before questions.

img.scene: A police officer speaking calmly to a seated person in an interview room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Miranda: rights before questions.
img.title: MIRANDA RIGHTS

questions.question: The right of a criminal defendant who cannot afford a lawyer to have one appointed was established in:
questions.explanation: Gideon held the Sixth Amendment right to counsel fundamental and binding on the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gideon: counsel for the poor.

img.scene: A public defender handing a folder to a client outside a courthouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Gideon: counsel for the poor.
img.title: GIDEON V WAINWRIGHT

questions.question: Students' free-speech rights at public school were addressed in Tinker v. Des Moines, where the Court protected wearing:
questions.correctAnswer: Black armbands protesting a war, absent substantial disruption
distractors: Any clothing at all without limits
Nothing - students lose all speech rights at school
questions.explanation: The Court said students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate; speech may be limited only on facts showing substantial disruption.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tinker: armbands protected.

img.scene: Students wearing plain black armbands walking in a school hallway. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Tinker: armbands protected.
img.title: TINKER V DES MOINES

questions.question: Flag burning as political protest was held to be protected symbolic speech in:
questions.explanation: Texas v. Johnson held that burning the flag as protest is expressive conduct protected by the First Amendment; the state may not ban it to preserve the flag as a symbol.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Johnson: flag burning is speech.

img.scene: A flag waving on a pole against a dramatic sky, viewed respectfully from below. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Johnson: flag burning is speech.
img.title: TEXAS V JOHNSON

questions.question: The Supreme Court case that incorporated most of the Bill of Rights against the states did so through which part of the Fourteenth Amendment?
distractors: The Privileges or Immunities Clause as the Court applied it in most cases
questions.explanation: Through selective incorporation, the Court has applied most Bill of Rights guarantees to the states as liberties protected by the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Incorporation runs through due process.

img.scene: A row of state capitol domes under one large arch. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Incorporation runs through due process.
img.title: INCORPORATION

questions.question: A trucking company argues Congress had no power to set rules for freight moving between states. Congress points to which constitutional source for that power?
questions.correctAnswer: The Commerce Clause, Article I, Section 8
questions.explanation: The Commerce Clause empowers Congress to regulate commerce among the states; Gibbons v. Ogden read it broadly as early as 1824.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Commerce Clause, Article One.

img.scene: Trucks and trains carrying goods across a river bridge between two states. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Commerce Clause, Article One.
img.title: COMMERCE CLAUSE

questions.question: A state proposes printing its own money and declaring war on a foreign power. Both ideas collide with the Constitution because those powers belong only to:
questions.explanation: Coinage and war declarations are enumerated federal powers; schools, licensing, and zoning are classic state and local functions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Coins and war: Congress only.

img.scene: Freshly minted coins spilling from a press tray. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Coins and war: Congress only.
img.title: ENUMERATED POWERS

questions.question: A state government may do all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.correctAnswer: Make a treaty with a foreign nation
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 10 bars states from treaties, coining money, and similar sovereign acts reserved to the Union.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: States cannot make treaties.

img.scene: A statehouse dome behind a fence line, symbolic boundary. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: States cannot make treaties.
img.title: STATE LIMITS

questions.question: Both Washington and Lincoln can levy taxes and fund highways at the same time. Political scientists give powers held simultaneously by both levels this name:
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers are held by both levels at once; denied powers are forbidden to one or both; reserved powers stay with the states.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Shared means concurrent.

img.scene: Two crews building the same road from opposite ends meeting in the middle. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Nebraska's two U.S. senators and its U.S. representatives are chosen by:
questions.correctAnswer: Nebraska voters in federal elections - the same voters who choose the state's nonpartisan legislators in separate races
questions.explanation: Federal officers are elected statewide (senators) and by congressional district (representatives). Those officeholders change with elections; the civics test's dynamic questions carry the current names.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Voters choose the federal delegation.

questions.question: A teacher places the two charters side by side. The Nebraska document stands out from the federal one chiefly because it:
questions.correctAnswer: Expressly reserves initiative, referendum, and recall powers and has been amended many times into a longer, more detailed document
distractors: Copies the federal text word for word
questions.explanation: Like many state charters, Nebraska's is longer and more policy-detailed than the federal Constitution and is amended frequently - including the 1934 amendment that created the unicameral itself.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: State charters run longer and closer.

questions.question: A Nebraska civics class visiting a meeting of their county board or city council is practicing exactly what 79-724 encourages:
questions.correctAnswer: First-hand study of the structure and function of local government in this state
distractors: A substitute for all classroom instruction
A federal requirement for graduation in every state
questions.explanation: The statute's local-government duty is why Nebraska classes study - and often attend - county and city meetings: local bodies are where most day-to-day governing touches residents.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Local government, seen up close.
